Object pronouns

Avoid repeating names and things: Call me, I know her, Give it to them, and Come with us.

≈ 55–65 min me / him / her / them after verbs and prepositions 11 interactive tasks
NoticeTrack people in a short exchange.
DiscoverMatch subject and object forms.
BuildReplace repeated nouns and things.
UseTalk about your real people.

Object pronouns keep your sentences short and natural: say a name once, then let me, him, her, it, us, and them do the work.

The system: subject and object pairs

Every subject pronoun has a partner form for the other side of the verb. Two of them, you and it, do not change at all.

subjectobjectexample
ImeCall me after the meeting.
youyouI can hear you clearly.
hehimI work with him.
sheherAsk her about the schedule.
ititI need it today.
weusCome with us.
theythemEmail them the address.

Use an object pronoun after a verb or a preposition: see her, for him, with them.

Get to the root: roles inside the sentence

A pronoun changes form because its role changes. The subject is the grammatical starting point, the person or thing connected to the verb before it. An object receives, experiences, or completes the action, or follows a preposition.

rolepositionquestion it answersexample
subjectnormally before the verbWho does or is this?They invited us.
object of a verbnormally after the verbWho or what receives it?They invited us.
object of a prepositionafter words such as to, for, withTo/for/with whom?Come with us.

Position: after the verb or after a preposition

Object pronouns live in two places: right after the verb, as in call me and I know him, or right after a preposition, as in listen to her, wait for us, and work with them. Before the verb, the subject slot still belongs to I, he, she, we, and they.

The classic error

I saw her. She saw me.

The same two people swap roles, and the forms swap with them. This is why I saw she is never possible: after the verb, only the object form works. At A1, keep it simple: before the verb, use I, he, she; after the verb or a preposition, use me, him, her.

It for a thing, them for plural things

Things follow the same system as people. Use it for one known thing and them for plural things: I love this song. Play it again. and I bought apples. Put them in the fridge. The listener recovers the thing from the sentence before.

Object pronouns with common verb patterns

Many everyday verbs take an object pronoun right after them, and some take two objects: a person and a thing.

patternexample
verb + objectCall me. I know him.
verb + object + thingSend her the link. Tell us the time.
verb + thing + to + objectSend the link to her. Give it to them.
preposition + objectWait for me. Sit next to him.

Pronouns are reference tools

A pronoun lets the listener recover a person or thing without repeating the full noun. The reference must be clear. I spoke to Maya and sent her the file is clear because her points back to Maya. If several women were mentioned, repeating the name may be clearer than using her.

Number and person must match the reference: one male person → him; one female person → her; one thing or animal when sex is not relevant → it; multiple people or things → them.

It, them, and one

Use it/them when referring to the same known thing or things: Where is my key? I need it. Use one/ones when you mean another example of that type: I need a key. Do you have one?

In careful standard usage, say between you and me, because a pronoun after a preposition takes the object form.

Drill 8: say it, then reveal

Read the cue, say the full sentence aloud with a pronoun, then reveal only after you answer.

2 We invited our neighbors. Replace “our neighbors.”

3 Do you know my brother? Replace “my brother.”

4 I can’t find my phone. Replace “my phone.”

Please send the file to us.

Wait for him downstairs.

Use it in real life

Your helpers: Name two people who help you, and say how you help them back. My coworker helps me with reports. I help her with English.
Your phone: Say four true sentences about your phone with it. I charge it at night. I check it too often.
Ask the teacher: Ask three questions with object pronouns and listen to the answers. Can you hear me? Who calls you every day?
Messages: Describe the messages you send in a normal day: who you send them to, and who answers you first.
Family: Say five sentences about family members with him, her, and them. I visit her on weekends. I call them from the car.

Reflect

Say the system back

Recite the seven pairs aloud: I → me, you → you, he → him, she → her, it → it, we → us, they → them. Then complete this aloud: “Before the verb, I use the ______ form. After the verb or a preposition, I use the ______ form.”

Finish with one true sentence about a person you will see today, using him or her.
